```jsonc
}
```

version = "0.1.0"
description = "Devboule — local agent orchestration dashboard"
edition = "2021"
license = "Apache-2.0"

# cannot infer which to launch. Pin the GUI binary as the default so `tauri dev`/`build`
# run the app; `claude_consent_hook` is built but only spawned explicitly by Claude Code.

[lib]
name = "devboule_lib"

# disables Cargo's auto-discovery of `src/main.rs` — without this entry the app binary

path = "src/main.rs"

# through the .aspis-agents.json consent file-bridge into the app's consent UI. The body
# lives in the lib (`run_claude_consent_hook`) so it reuses the same file-lock +
# serializer; this bin is a thin shim. Declared explicitly so it builds alongside the
# default `devboule` GUI binary (src/main.rs).
[[bin]]
name = "claude_consent_hook"
path = "src/bin/claude_consent_hook.rs"

[features]
default = []

[build-dependencies]
tauri-build = { version = "2", features = [] }

[dependencies]
tauri = { version = "2", features = [] }
libc = "0.2" # process-group kill for the sandboxed `run` tool timeout (unix)
tauri-plugin-dialog = "2"
tauri-plugin-notification = "2"
serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }
serde_json = { version = "1", features = ["preserve_order"] }
regex = "1"
chrono = { version = "0.4", features = ["serde"] }

# to the in-memory `mock` store, where `set_password` returns Ok but the secret is
# kept only inside that one `Entry` object — a freshly constructed `Entry::new`
# returns `NoEntry`. That made EVERY vault credential (Oracle LLM key, provider
# tokens, device keys) appear to save yet never persist (Bug B). Enable the
# platform-native OS keystores; keyring compiles only the one matching the build
# target, so listing both is the correct Windows+macOS setup.
keyring = { version = "3.6", features = ["windows-native", "apple-native"] }
open = "5.3"
reqwest = { version = "0.12", default-features = false, features = ["blocking", "json", "rustls-tls", "stream"] }

# HTTP generation reads `reqwest::Response::bytes_stream()` on the shared async client,
# and the buffered CLI path spawns + (on cancel) kills a child via `tokio::process`.
# tokio is ALREADY in the tree transitively (via tauri); listing it directly with this
# feature subset is purely additive feature unification — no new top-level crate.

urlencoding = "2.1"
sha2 = "0.10"
hex = "0.4"
getrandom = "0.3"
futures-util = "0.3"
fs2 = "0.4"
x25519-dalek = { version = "2", features = ["static_secrets"] }
ed25519-dalek = { version = "2", features = ["rand_core"] }
rand_core = { version = "0.6", features = ["getrandom"] }
aes-gcm = "0.10"
hkdf = "0.12"
tar = "0.4"
zeroize = "1.8"
subtle = "2.6"
uuid = { version = "1", features = ["v4"] }
notify = "6"
sysinfo = { version = "0.33", default-features = false, features = ["system"] }

# args choice at spawn time is. Same stack/crate as the studied terax-ai (Apache-2.0).

# `tree-sitter >=0.21,<0.23`, which would pull a SECOND `tree-sitter` runtime and break
# the single-tree-sitter invariant; the `-ng` fork uses the modern
# `tree-sitter-language ^0.1` normal dep (`tree-sitter` DEV-only `^0.24`), so it links
# against the SAME 0.25 runtime — `cargo tree -i tree-sitter` stays ONE.
tree-sitter = "0.25"
tree-sitter-rust = "0.24"
tree-sitter-typescript = "0.23"
tree-sitter-python = "0.25"
tree-sitter-go = "0.25"
tree-sitter-cpp = "0.23"
tree-sitter-html = "0.23"
tree-sitter-kotlin-ng = "1.1"

# (`apply_emitted_edits` in backend/mini_coder_executor.rs). `TextDiff::ratio()` is a
# faithful Rust port of Python difflib's `SequenceMatcher.ratio()` — the SAME metric
# Aider uses for its near-miss splice fallback — so the similarity tier matches that
# well-trodden behavior rather than a hand-rolled Levenshtein ratio. Pure-Rust,
# MIT/Apache-2.0, GPU-free. `default-features = false, features = ["text"]` keeps only
# the line/char diff + ratio machinery (drops bytes/unicode/inline/serde/web-time).
similar = { version = "2", default-features = false, features = ["text"] }

# a path dep so the app can host `oracle_core::server::serve` in-process on the
# loopback port. Base dep has no `metal` (Windows/Linux stay ORT CPU). On macOS
# we re-declare with `features = ["metal"]` so Candle can use the Metal device
# (see rust_oracle embed backend selection). BUILD: lancedb needs protoc.
oracle-core = { path = "../oracle-core" }

# Windows-only WinRT/Win32 bindings. All `use windows::` call sites in src/ are
# `#[cfg(windows)]`-gated, so target-gate the crate too: it is never fetched or
# built on macOS/Linux.
[target.'cfg(windows)'.dependencies]
windows = { version = "0.58", features = ["Foundation", "Security_Credentials_UI", "Win32_Foundation", "Win32_Graphics_Dxgi", "Win32_Graphics_Dxgi_Common", "Win32_Storage_FileSystem", "Win32_System_Threading", "Win32_System_WinRT", "Win32_UI_WindowsAndMessaging"] }

# `design-preview` window. `webview2-com` is pinned to the EXACT version already in the
# tree transitively (via wry/tauri) so its `ICoreWebView2*` types are identical to the

# tree). The crate is brought in under the RENAMED package `windows_capture` so it
# coexists with the existing `windows = 0.58` above (two `windows` versions, distinct
# extern-crate names — no conflict); 0.61.3 == webview2-com's exact version, so the
# `IStream` we create is the same monomorphic type `CapturePreview` accepts.
webview2-com = "=0.38.2"
windows_capture = { package = "windows", version = "=0.61.3", features = ["Win32_Foundation", "Win32_System_Com", "Win32_System_Com_StructuredStorage"] }

# macOS: Touch ID (LocalAuthentication) + Candle Metal for Oracle embeddings.
# `oracle-core/metal` is compile-error on non-macOS — only enable here.
# ORT CoreML cannot run the Qwen3 ONNX export; Metal via Candle is the GPU path.
[target.'cfg(target_os = "macos")'.dependencies]
objc2 = "0.5"
objc2-foundation = { version = "0.2", features = ["NSString", "NSError"] }
# "block2" unlocks evaluatePolicy_localizedReason_reply (the async reply-block
# API used by backend/auth.rs verify_user).
objc2-local-authentication = { version = "0.2", features = ["LAContext", "LAError", "block2"] }
block2 = "0.5"
oracle-core = { path = "../oracle-core", features = ["metal"] }

content.thinking:
Three more critical findings:

**Finding 1: ort version coexistence — the amendment is wrong about the migration direction.**
- The plan §0 (original) said: "ort w/ directml feature on Windows; keep candle-metal on macOS". The plan treated DirectML on Windows as net-new.
- The actual `oracle-core/Cargo.toml` shows: Windows branch already has `ort = { version = "2.0.0-rc.10", features = ["directml"] }`. macOS branch has `ort = { version = "2.0.0-rc.10", features = ["coreml"] }`. Linux branch has `ort = { version = "2.0.0-rc.10" }` (no EP feature).
- **DirectML is already wired at RC10.** The plan was wrong about this being new work. Milestone F is mostly already done.
- The amendment's §A snippet proposing `default-features = false, features = ["std", "ndarray", "directml"]` would **BREAK the build** by dropping `download-binaries` (confirmed by Exa search result quoting `ort.pyke.io/setup/cargo-features`: "Disabling this means you'll need to compile ONNX Runtime from source yourself"). Devboule currently relies on default features including `download-binaries`.
- The amendment drops the Linux/other target block (`target.'cfg(not(any(target_os = "macos", target_os = "windows")))'`). Actual file has this block. Dropping it means Linux falls back to the top-level `[dependencies]` block which... wait, the amendment's snippet DOES have a top-level `[dependencies]` ort line. So Linux would get `std, ndarray` only — no EP. That's actually OK as a fallback but is different behavior from the current "no EP features" setup, which... hmm. Actually `features = ["std", "ndarray"]` on Linux would work as CPU-only. But it changes the defaults. Currently devboule uses default features (which include `download-binaries`, `tls-native`, `tracing`, `copy-dylibs`, `api-24` per my earlier search). The amendment's `default-features = false, features = ["std", "ndarray"]` DROPS all those. **Definitely a build break.**

**Finding 2: ort RC10 wraps ONNX Runtime 1.22, RC12 wraps ONNX Runtime 1.24.**
- Confirmed via Exa: `ort 2.0.0-rc.10 - Docs.rs: A safe Rust wrapper for ONNX Runtime 1.22`. And `ort 2.0.0-rc.12 - Docs.rs: A safe Rust wrapper for ONNX Runtime 1.24`.
- The amendment's §A claim "Both RCs target the same ONNX Runtime 1.24 underneath" is **FALSE**. RC10 → ORT 1.22, RC12 → ORT 1.24.
- This means the version bump from rc.10→rc.12 is NOT a minor change — it bumps the underlying ONNX Runtime major.minor (1.22 → 1.24). DirectML EP behavior, model format support, operator coverage could all change. **The amendment completely glosses over this risk.**

**Finding 3: fastembed 5.x also uses ort.**
- Confirmed via Exa: `fastembed 5.17.2` depends on `ort` (it's listed in deps). The exact version fastembed pins would determine whether devboule's workspace has ort version conflicts.
- devboule's `oracle-core/Cargo.toml` declares `fastembed = { version = "5", features = ["qwen3"] }` AND `ort = { version = "2.0.0-rc.10", features = ["coreml"] }` (macOS).
- **If fastembed pins ort to a different version (e.g., `^2.0.0-rc.10` vs `^2.0.0-rc.12`), Cargo's semver resolver will pick one and may conflict.** This is a real workspace risk the plan doesn't mention.

**Finding 4: Cargo.toml line numbering.** The amendment §D says "devboule's existing `Cargo.toml:55` declaration is correct". Looking at the actual file, keyring is indeed declared in [dependencies] but I need to confirm the exact line. Let me count... actually the file shows the keyring comment block is extensive. Let me not claim line 55 without verification.

**Finding 5: The `windows` crate version mismatch.**
- devboule's `src-tauri/Cargo.toml` uses `windows = "0.58"` (under `[target.'cfg(windows)'.dependencies]`).
- The plan §4.1 proposes adding `windows = { version = "0.62", features = [...] }` for the sandbox primitives.
- **Two different `windows` crate versions in one crate** (0.58 for existing UI/auth + 0.62 for sandbox). This may or may not work depending on whether types cross boundaries. The plan doesn't acknowledge this. Also: the plan's feature list includes `Win32_Security_Credentials` but the existing dep uses `Security_Credentials_UI` (note the `_UI` suffix). These are different features.
- ALSO: `webview2-com = "=0.38.2"` + `windows_capture = { package = "windows", version = "=0.61.3", features = [...] }`. So devboule ALREADY has TWO windows crate versions (0.58 and 0.61.3-renamed). Adding 0.62 would make it THREE. This is getting messy.

**Finding 6: tauri.conf.json — `beforeBuildCommand` uses bash.**
- The actual `tauri.conf.json` has `"beforeBuildCommand": "bash -c '...' && bash scripts/stage-devboule-mcp.sh && npm run build"`.
- **This `bash` invocation won't work on Windows without WSL/Git Bash.** Tauri's Windows builds run `beforeBuildCommand` via the system shell, which on Windows is cmd.exe or PowerShell, not bash.
- **Neither the plan nor the amendment addresses this.** This is a real Windows build blocker that's way more important than `bundle.windows` block details. The plan's Milestone A (adding `bundle.windows`) won't actually produce a working Windows installer because `beforeBuildCommand` will fail.

This is a BLOCKER. Let me verify by web_search.

**Finding 7: Bundle resources use forward-slash paths.**
- `resources: ["../oracle", "resources/censor/semgrep-rules.yml", "resources/oracle-models", "../pi-sidecar/*"]`
- These relative paths use forward slashes which Tauri normalizes cross-platform. OK.
- BUT: `../oracle` and `../pi-sidecar/*` reference directories OUTSIDE `src-tauri/`. On Windows, these need to exist at build time. **The plan doesn't verify these exist or that they're Windows-compatible.**

**Finding 8: `externalBin: ["binaries/devboule-mcp"]`** — this is a Tauri external binary. On Windows, Tauri expects `binaries/devboule-mcp-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc.exe`. The plan doesn't mention building/providing this binary for Windows.

**Finding 9: Sandbox mod.rs `is_enforced()` docstring contradicts the amendment.**
- The actual code comment at `mod.rs` says: "Forward-compatible: when the Windows Job Object backend lands (sandbox epic phase 3 — Restricted Token + WFP + Job Object, the `#[cfg(not(target_os = "macos"))]` passthrough branch in `wrap`), Windows go-live is JUST flipping the `windows` arm below to `true`. No other code changes."
- This comment claims flipping `is_enforced()` to true is "JUST" flipping the bool — "No other code changes." But the amendment correctly identifies that this is NOT true: you need C1+C2+C3+C4 (job, token, ACL, network) before flipping is safe.
- **The amendment correctly identifies a real security lie in the existing code comment.** But the amendment doesn't propose updating the comment. It should.

**Finding 10: Seatbelt deny-default vs srt-win allow-default semantics.**
- The amendment §B correctly identifies this: Seatbelt uses `(deny default)` then explicit allows. srt-win uses allow-default with explicit denies.
- For devboule's `readonly_root` (project root, NEVER writable): on macOS, the Seatbelt profile denies ALL writes by default, then allows only `writable_paths`. The `readonly_root` is implicitly denied because it's not in the allowlist.
- On Windows with srt-win-style ACLs: the `srt-sandbox` user has NO inherent permissions. Files owned by the primary user are NOT writable by `srt-sandbox` unless explicitly granted. So `readonly_root` is implicitly denied because no `allowWrite` ACE is stamped on it.
- **This is actually equivalent semantics** — both deny-by-default, just via different mechanisms (Seatbelt profile vs ACL inheritance).
- BUT: the amendment's concern about "a sandboxed process can still WRITE to anything that isn't on policy.writable_paths if the parent directory allows it" is valid IF the sandbox runs as the SAME user as the broker. srt-win avoids this by using a DEDICATED `srt-sandbox` user. If devboule's Windows sandbox runs as the same user (no user-switching), then ACL inheritance from the user's own directories would allow writes everywhere. **The amendment doesn't address whether devboule should provision a dedicated sandbox user.** That's the load-bearing question.

**Finding 11: `wrap()` return type is `SandboxedCommand { program, args }`.**
- The plan's C1 says "ship a `windows_apply_sandbox_to_command(cmd: &mut Command, policy: &SandboxPolicy)` function the spawner calls before `.spawn()`." This is a DIFFERENT API than `wrap()` which returns `SandboxedCommand`.
- The amendment doesn't address this API mismatch. The macOS path uses `wrap()` → returns `SandboxedCommand` → spawner builds `Command` from it → calls `apply_rlimits()`. The Windows path would need either (a) `wrap()` returning a pass-through `SandboxedCommand` + a separate `windows_apply_sandbox_to_command()` call, or (b) `wrap()` returning a wrapped command like macOS.
- Option (a) means `wrap()` is a no-op on Windows and the real work happens in a separate function. That's a different architecture than macOS. The plan acknowledges this ("keeps wrap() returning a thin pass-through") but doesn't address how callers know to call `windows_apply_sandbox_to_command()`. The spawner code needs updating.

OK I have enough for a thorough hostile review. Let me also do a couple more targeted searches to confirm the tauri beforeBuildCommand issue and the windows crate multi-version issue.
